content.thinking:
I'm writing up the symptom first: account pages failed for many shoppers. For the causal chain, I'm tying that failure to the error rate on account pages, citing the two metrics Gbac1 and G5309, and I'm weighing whether the alert series AL1 belongs in there too.

I'm working through the causal chain now, linking the account page failures to a division error in the spend summary code, then tracing why requests reached that code path after the legacy fallback was switched off.

I'm checking the remaining candidates for the trigger: the monthly-spend switch was already ruled out, since turning it off didn't bring the service back, and I'm finding no deploys in the window that could explain the change.

I'm checking the mechanism for the last step: the spend summary divides by the number of this month's purchases, which is empty for shoppers who bought nothing this month, so the division by zero fires. The log line confirms the division error at line 47, but not why the divisor is empty; that part rests on the code reading, which I haven't run.

I'm ordering the chain now: the ZeroDivisionError at line 47 comes first, then the switch to the new renderer after the flag was turned off, and the last step is the division by an empty count of this month's purchases.

I'm settling the root cause: once the legacy fallback was off, requests went down the new renderer path, where the spend summary divides by this month's purchase count, which is empty for any shopper who hasn't bought anything this month. I'll keep it framed as my reading of the code, since I haven't run it.

I'm drafting the plain-language cause and the still-at-risk note now, keeping each claim to what the record supports, and starting the contributing factors list.

I'm laying out the contributing factors now: the flag was switched off for all traffic at once with no staged rollout or error-rate guard visible, and no test seems to have covered the spend summary for shoppers with no purchases this month before that path went live.

I'm now listing the contributing factors, noting that the flag was switched off for all traffic at once with no staged rollout or error-rate guard, and that no pre-change test appears to have exercised the flag-gated path for shoppers with no purchases this month. I'm also noting that nobody was paged by the alert, which I'm treating as a separate detection gap.

I'm adding the paging gap as its own contributing factor: the alert never reached an on-call person, so nobody was engaged at the start. I'm also noting that two flags were toggled at the same instant by one admin, so the logs couldn't separate their effects and the first mitigation pick went the wrong way.

I'm listing the action items now: one to stage flag changes behind a rollout that reverts when errors climb, one to run a pre-change test over the code paths a flag switch turns on, and one to route the HighErrorRate alert to an on-call rotation so someone gets paged.

I'm listing the paging gap and the flag changes made at the same instant as contributing factors, then moving to the lessons. For what went well, I'm noting that the reversions were reversible, the fix draft was proposed, and the mitigation brought the service back.

I'm checking the last items in the review: the investigation ranked the monthly-spend candidate above the legacy-fallback lead and acted on it first, so the first revert didn't help and cost several minutes. The response itself went fine, and I'm leaving the page-gap point out since it's already covered.

I'm settling the assumptions: the mechanism comes from reading the code and nothing has been run, which the write-up already says, and since the history doesn't name the revision, I'm taking the source Code-Fix read to be the revision the replicas were running.

I'm noting that the sample of ZeroDivisionError lines is supporting evidence for the cause, and I'm checking that the first step still cites the two error-rate metrics without adding figures. The chain holds together, so I'm marking both the cause and the reliance on the code reading as settled.

action_items.item: Put flag changes on io-shop behind a staged rollout that widens step by step and switches back on its own when the account page error rate rises.
Before any flag switch goes to production, run tests that exercise the code path the switch turns on, including shoppers with no purchases in the current month.
Require flag changes on the same service to go out one at a time, with the service checked between them.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed: the error rate on account pages went up and stayed up.
The failing account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47.

Account pages were no longer served by the legacy renderer. The new renderer served them instead, and that path reaches the failing spend-summary code. This followed legacy-checkout-fallback reading off in the flag evaluations.

ruled_out.what: Feature flag monthly-spend-feature, which the same admin switched on at the same instant: turning it back off left the service at the incident's level, so it was put back.
A deploy: the read of production changes found no deploys, only the two flag changes.

causal_chain.step: An admin switched feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback off.
On that path, the spend summary divides the month's total by the number of purchases this month, and that list is empty for any shopper who has bought nothing this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: An administrator switched off an older fallback for showing shoppers their account pages, which sent those pages through newer code that most likely breaks when it works out a shopper's average spend for the month if they have bought nothing that month.

contributing_factors.factor: No staged rollout or automatic guard was seen on the flag change. legacy-checkout-fallback went from on to off for all account page traffic within the minute it was switched.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A staged switch that watched the error rate would have stopped at a small share of shoppers and switched back, before most account pages failed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that exercised the code path a flag switch turns on before the switch was made in production. Here that path was the new renderer's spend summary for a shopper with no purchases this month.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division fault would have shown up before the flag was switched, and the switch would not have gone out.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: Two flags on the same service were switched by the same admin at the same instant, so the logs could not separate their effects.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: With the flags changed one at a time, the errors would have lined up with the one change that caused them, and the right flag could have been reverted first, shortening the incident.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to an on-call rotation, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been brought in when the alert fired, able to weigh the leads alongside Argus and step in if the automated response went wrong.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

lead_effects.effect: It did not change what was done: the investigation weighed it as unverified and reverted monthly-spend-feature first, and reverted legacy-checkout-fallback, the flag the lead named, only after the first action was refuted; that revert was confirmed, so the lead proved right.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent weighed the person's lead in the thread against the record and noted that both flags had changed at the same instant, keeping legacy-checkout-fallback as a candidate.
The Mitigation Agent put monthly-spend-feature back when reverting it did not help, so the refuted action left nothing changed behind it.
The Mitigation Agent switched legacy-checkout-fallback back on, which put the service back.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #549.
Every action taken was a flag revert that could be put back.

went_wrong: The response acted first on monthly-spend-feature, the higher-ranked candidate, even though the person's lead named legacy-checkout-fallback. That revert did not help, and account pages kept failing until the second flag was reverted.

input.root_cause: With legacy-checkout-fallback off, account pages took a path where `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py` divides the month's total by the number of purchases this month. That list is empty for any shopper who has bought nothing this month, so the division raised ZeroDivisionError at line 47, and `serve_account_page` turned each one into a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: If anyone switches legacy-checkout-fallback off again, account pages could fail again for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
